title: Shared cell ancestry inflates apparent skill in a cell-response model
summary: In a retrospective audit of STATE, mean correlation on expected-null cases in one donor fell from 0.260 with reference cells sharing ancestry to 0.005 with independently sampled references, against 0.081 for a context-mean baseline. The model also fell below baseline with independent references in three additional donors. The finding concerns apparent predictive skill under the tested evaluation design.

source_review.scope: arXiv v1 front matter, section 2.7, Figure 7, relative baseline comparison and non-operational evaluation of reported model outcomes

evidence.tested: The audit compared reference overlap conditions, with equal reference sample sizes and the same learned predictions. The primary quantitative comparison uses one donor, with follow-up STATE comparisons across four available donors.
evidence.unknown: This retrospective audit characterizes the tested data and model, with expected-null cases defined operationally. It does not measure biological benefit or imply all transfer estimates are inflated.
evidence.ai_role: The trained STATE transfer model generated cell-response estimates whose accuracy could be compared against overlapping and independent reference samples.
